results.question: What is the official name and number of the DPDP Act?
results.answer: The official name is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and it is Act No. 22 of 2023.

results.question: When did the President give assent to the Act?
results.answer: The President gave assent to the Act on 11 August 2023.

results.question: Is the whole DPDP Act in force today?
results.answer: No. As of 25 October 2026, the Act is only partly in force: some provisions are already in force, while others start on 13 November 2026 and 13 May 2027.
details: The foundations and Data Protection Board provisions have been in force since 13 November 2025.
The provisions allowing Consent Managers to register start on 13 November 2026.
The main duties, rights and penalties start on 13 May 2027.

results.question: Which provisions came into force on 13 November 2025?
results.answer: On 13 November 2025, section 1(2), section 2, sections 18–26, 35 and 38–43, and section 44(1) and (3) came into force.
details: Rules 1, 2 and 17–21 also came into force on publication.

results.question: What starts on 13 November 2026?
results.answer: On 13 November 2026, section 6(9) and section 27(1)(d) start, allowing Consent Managers to register.

results.question: When do the main obligations on businesses start?
results.answer: The main duties are scheduled to start on 13 May 2027. They are not yet in force as of 25 October 2026.
details: The commencement notification sets that date for sections 3–17 and other provisions; a separate Consent Manager provision starts earlier, on 13 November 2026.

results.question: Are people's rights to access and erase their data in force yet?
results.answer: Not yet: sections 11–17, which include the relevant rights, are scheduled to start on 13 May 2027. The Act identifies erasure as a Data Principal’s right.
results.uncertainty: The supplied Act excerpt identifies the right to erasure but does not reproduce the access-right provision; the commencement notification schedules sections 11–17 to start later.

results.question: Within how many hours must a data breach be reported to the Board?
results.answer: Not yet: the breach-reporting duty starts on 13 May 2027.
details: Once it applies, the Board must receive an initial description without delay, followed by fuller details within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach. The Board may allow longer on a written request.

results.question: What is the maximum penalty for failing to take reasonable security safeguards?
results.answer: The maximum penalty is up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards.
details: The main duties and penalties start on 13 May 2027; they are not in force today.

results.question: What must a privacy notice contain under the Rules?
results.answer: Under Rule 3, the notice must stand on its own, use clear and plain language, itemise the personal data, state the specific purpose, and describe the goods, services or uses involved.
details: It must also give the particular link to the Data Fiduciary’s website or app and describe any other means for the relevant purpose.
These Rules start on 13 May 2027; they are not yet in force as of 25 October 2026.
results.uncertainty: The retrieved excerpt ends before completing the final requirement about other means.

results.question: Who counts as a Data Fiduciary?
results.answer: A Data Fiduciary is any person who, alone or with others, decides why and how personal data is processed.
details: The Act’s definition is in force since 13 November 2025.

results.question: Does the Act apply to a foreign company that serves customers in India?
results.answer: Not yet: the Act covers a foreign company’s processing of digital personal data when it is connected to offering goods or services to people in India, but this rule starts on 13 May 2027.
details: As of 25 October 2026, that scope rule is not yet in force; the main duties, rights and penalties start on 13 May 2027.
results.uncertainty: Whether a particular company’s processing meets the Act’s test depends on the facts: the text does not settle that for a specific company.

results.question: Who counts as a child under the Act and what is needed to process their data?
results.answer: A child is anyone under 18. The retrieved passages point to verifiable consent under section 9(1), but do not show the full consent requirement; they do say child-data processing must not involve tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children.
details: The Act’s child-data duties, including section 9, start on 13 May 2027. They are not yet in force today, 25 October 2026.
The Act defines a child’s Data Principal to include the child’s parent or lawful guardian.
results.uncertainty: The retrieved passages do not set out who must provide verifiable consent or the precise steps and conditions for obtaining it.

notes: Statement 3: The excerpt includes a child’s parent, but does not show that a lawful guardian is included.

results.question: Is there an automatic exemption for startups?
results.answer: No: There is no automatic startup exemption. The Government may exempt startups or other notified classes from specified provisions by notification.
details: Anvaya has not found an official notification granting this exemption.
The startup-exemption provision, section 17(3), starts on 13 May 2027.

results.question: What is a Consent Manager and when can one register?
results.answer: A Consent Manager is a Board-registered intermediary that lets a person give, manage, review and withdraw consent through one platform. Registration can begin on 13 November 2026.
details: An eligible person may apply to the Board; the Board can register the applicant or reject the application. The registration conditions are set out in Part A of the First Schedule.
results.uncertainty: The retrieved passages do not set out the specific conditions in Part A of the First Schedule.

results.question: How long must a company keep logs of how it processes personal data?
results.answer: From 13 May 2027, a company acting as a Data Fiduciary must keep processing logs for at least one year from the date of processing.
details: After that, the logs must be erased unless another law requires longer retention or the Government has notified otherwise.
This retention rule is not yet in force as of 25 October 2026; it starts on 13 May 2027.

notes: Statement 1: The one-year retention duty and start date are supported, but the passage limits it to purposes specified in the Seventh Schedule.

results.question: What changed in the Act in October 2026?
results.answer: In October 2026, a Removal of Difficulties Order made two wording fixes to the Act: one in section 9(1), and one in section 10(2)(c)(ii).
details: Section 9(1) was changed to say “child or of a person with disability.”
Section 10(2)(c)(ii) was changed from “audit” to “data audit.”
The Order describes these as textual and editorial corrections.

results.question: What does the Act say about transferring personal data outside India?
results.answer: Not yet in force: the transfer framework starts on 13 May 2027. When it starts, transfers may be restricted or made subject to government-set conditions; it is not framed as a blanket ban.
details: The Act allows the Central Government to restrict transfers to specified countries or territories by notification. It also preserves any Indian law that provides stronger protection or tighter transfer restrictions.

The Rules allow transfers subject to requirements the Central Government may specify for making personal data available to a foreign State, or to a person or entity controlled by or acting for that State.

For Significant Data Fiduciaries, government-specified personal data and related traffic data must not be transferred outside India. This rule starts with the main duties on 13 May 2027; Anvaya has not found an official notification designating a Significant Data Fiduciary.
results.uncertainty: The retrieved passages do not identify any country-specific restrictions or government orders specifying transfer requirements.

results.question: Has the Government officially cut the 18-month deadline to 12 months?
results.answer: No: Anvaya has not found an official notification changing the deadline. The official schedule still sets the main duties and rights to start on 13 May 2027, eighteen months after publication of the commencement notification.
details: The commencement notification specifies that the main provisions come into force eighteen months after its publication.
results.uncertainty: Reports of a possible shortening of the 18-month period are unconfirmed.

results.question: Since the Act came into force in 2023, what penalty applies to my customer data breach today?
results.answer: No: the DPDP Act’s customer-data breach duties and related penalties are not in force today; they are scheduled to start on 13 May 2027.
details: When those provisions start, the Act sets a maximum penalty of ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failing to notify a breach.
